sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation and Initial Diagnostic Challenge
sections.description: This section introduces the patient's presentation with progressive neck swelling and proximal muscle weakness, the initial emergency department and ENT evaluations, and the evolving clinical suspicion from Ludwig's angina to idiopathic angioedema. It covers the key features that made the presentation atypical for angioedema and the critical clinical observations—including subtle cutaneous signs and nailfold capillaroscopy findings—that prompted further immunological evaluation. A brief overview of histamine-mediated and bradykinin-mediated angioedema is provided to contextualize why this presentation did not fit either mechanism.
subtopics: Presenting symptoms: 3-week history of progressive neck swelling, proximal muscle weakness, and mild myalgia
Initial emergency department assessment: vital signs, inflammatory markers, and suspicion of Ludwig's angina
CT neck findings: diffuse neck edema involving strap muscles and retropharyngeal space inflammation
ENT evaluation: flexible nasendoscopy findings and exclusion of structural or infectious causes
Referral to clinical immunology for suspected idiopathic angioedema
Overview of angioedema: histaminergic vs bradykinin-mediated mechanisms and their typical clinical features
Features atypical for angioedema: absence of trigger medications, no personal or family history, erythematous non-tender swelling, associated skin and muscle findings
Key physical examination findings: facial erythema, periungual erythema, rash on lateral thigh, reduced hip flexor power
Nailfold capillaroscopy findings: microhaemorrhages and avascular areas as early clues to a connective tissue disorder

sections.description: This section covers the systematic approach to the differential diagnosis of subacute neck swelling with constitutional symptoms, and the clinical reasoning process that redirected the diagnostic trajectory from angioedema to dermatomyositis. It explains how the combination of subtle cutaneous signs, proximal muscle weakness, and markedly elevated creatine kinase formed a coherent diagnostic picture. The section also introduces the concept of pseudoangioedema in inflammatory myopathies and contrasts it with true angioedema.
subtopics: Broad differential diagnosis for subacute neck swelling with elevated CRP
Infectious causes: Ludwig's angina, deep neck space infections, cellulitis, bacterial sialadenitis
Angioedema: hereditary, acquired, drug-induced, and idiopathic subtypes
Other inflammatory and vascular causes: orofacial granulomatosis, hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis, superior vena cava syndrome
Neuromuscular and drug hypersensitivity differentials: myasthenia gravis, DRESS syndrome, contact dermatitis
The pivotal role of creatine kinase testing: how an elevated CK of 16,184 U/L redirected the diagnostic workup
Interpretation of elevated muscle enzymes (CK, AST, ALT, LDH) in the context of inflammatory myopathy
How subtle skin findings (periungual erythema, facial erythema, Holster sign) combined with muscle weakness pointed to dermatomyositis
Pseudoangioedema in dermatomyositis: mechanism and distinction from histamine/bradykinin-mediated angioedema
Recognizing that dysphagia and muscle weakness may be subtle or overlooked in the context of prominent neck swelling

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology of Dermatomyositis and Anti-SAE1 Antibody Disease
sections.description: This section provides the essential pathophysiological background on dermatomyositis, focusing on its immunopathogenesis as a complement-mediated vasculopathy, the role of type I interferons, and the significance of myositis-specific antibodies—particularly anti-SAE1. It explains how these mechanisms produce the characteristic clinical features including skin manifestations, muscle inflammation, dysphagia, and the rare phenomenon of subcutaneous edema or pseudoangioedema. The section connects disease mechanisms to the patient's specific presentation.
subtopics: Dermatomyositis as an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy: epidemiology and bimodal age distribution
Immunopathogenesis: complement-mediated microvasculopathy affecting endomysial capillaries with C5b-9 deposition
Role of type I interferon signature in dermatomyositis and its link to cutaneous and systemic manifestations
Myositis-specific antibodies and their associations with distinct clinical phenotypes
Anti-SAE1 antibodies: target antigen (SUMO activating enzyme), role in sumoylation, and disease phenotype
Clinical features of anti-SAE1 dermatomyositis: cutaneous manifestations, dysphagia (46%), interstitial lung disease (43%), malignancy risk (18%)
Characteristic cutaneous manifestations of dermatomyositis: Gottron's papules, heliotrope eruption, shawl sign, V-neck sign, Holster sign, periungual changes
Mechanism of subcutaneous edema in dermatomyositis: muscle inflammation leading to soft tissue swelling rather than vascular permeability
Why pseudoangioedema is uncommon (6.6% of dermatomyositis patients) and which antibodies are more commonly associated with it

sections.description: This section details the comprehensive diagnostic workup that confirmed dermatomyositis and characterized the full extent of disease. It covers autoantibody profiling, imaging studies (MRI, FDG-PET, CT chest), muscle biopsy histopathology, swallow assessment, pulmonary evaluation, and the rationale for malignancy screening based on risk stratification. The section explains how each investigation contributed to confirming the diagnosis, assessing organ involvement, and planning treatment.
subtopics: Complement studies (C3, C4, C1 esterase function and quantification) to definitively exclude hereditary and acquired angioedema
Autoantibody profile: ANA (1:1280 speckled), ANCA negativity, and myositis antibody panel via Euroimmun Euroline immunoassay
Anti-SAE1 antibody positivity: signal intensity 173 (normal <35) and negativity for other myositis-specific antibodies
MRI of thighs: characteristic findings of active myositis in obturator internus/externus, hip adductors, gracilis, and distal iliopsoas
FDG-PET scan: diffuse abnormal FDG accumulation in multiple muscle groups and exclusion of metabolically active malignancy
Muscle biopsy histopathology: perifascicular necrotic and regenerative myofibers, perimysial inflammation, and C5b-9 deposition in perifascicular endomysial capillaries
Video fluoroscopic swallow study: severe pharyngeal dysphagia with pyriform fossae residue and post-swallow aspiration
Pulmonary function tests and CT chest: extrathoracic restrictive pattern, pulmonary nodules, peribronchial consolidation from aspiration
Malignancy risk stratification using IMACS guidelines: high-risk factors (dermatomyositis, dysphagia) and intermediate risk factors (SAE1 positive, male sex)
Malignancy screening strategy: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, PET scan, tumor markers, and planned GI endoscopy
Pre-immunosuppression infection screening: hepatitis B/C, HIV, VZV, CMV serology, and QuantiFERON-TB Gold

sections.description: This section covers the multidisciplinary treatment strategy, including the rationale for selecting specific immunosuppressive agents, the management of treatment-related complications, and the patient's clinical course from hospitalization through long-term follow-up. It concludes with the clinical lessons from the case, emphasizing the importance of considering dermatomyositis in the differential diagnosis of unexplained neck swelling, the value of a targeted creatine kinase test, and the need for prompt aggressive immunosuppression in severe disease.
subtopics: Treatment rationale: significant airway and swallowing muscle involvement necessitating aggressive immunosuppression
Corticosteroid therapy: IV methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 3 days followed by oral prednisone tapering regimen
Intravenous immunoglobulin: loading dose 2 g/kg over 5 days followed by maintenance cycles every 4 weeks
Steroid-sparing immunosuppression: mycophenolate mofetil selection and rationale over methotrexate (pulmonary concerns), azathioprine, and tacrolimus
Rituximab: two doses of 1000 mg IV two weeks apart for B-cell depletion in severe disease
Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis: sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim cessation due to hemolytic anemia and switch to nebulized pentamidine
Inpatient course: 21-day hospitalization, nasogastric tube feeding for persistent dysphagia
Short-term outcomes: moderate improvement in hip flexor weakness, marked improvement in cervical swelling, persistence of dysphagia requiring NG tube for 2 months
Medium-term outcomes: full recovery of proximal muscle strength, CK normalization, NG tube removal, resolution of cervical swelling by 3 months
Long-term outcomes: prednisone discontinuation at 7 months, near-complete resolution of pulmonary findings at 11 months, stable respiratory function at 12 months
Ongoing management plan: continuation of IVIG, mycophenolate tapering, and malignancy surveillance

Clinical lessons: dermatomyositis as a differential for unexplained neck swelling, importance of CK testing, need for careful skin and nailfold examination, and value of multidisciplinary collaboration
